chunks: "Almost every IC supply wants decoupling, so the exceptions are specific.

First, when the datasheet says not to, or limits it: some LDOs need a minimum ESR for stability, so a big low-ESR ceramic makes them oscillate; precision references and op-amp outputs often have a maximum capacitive load, beyond which they ring or oscillate; and some parts have integrated capacitors or are designed capacitor-free.
Second, when the capacitor creates a new problem.

On a hot-plugged input, a low-ESR ceramic with the cable inductance forms an underdamped series RLC, and the capacitor voltage can overshoot to nearly twice the input, so I'd use damping, a bulk electrolytic or a TVS, rather than just more ceramics.
Large capacitors on a battery or hot-swap rail cause inrush currents, C dV/dt, that trip protection. Mixing values badly can create an anti-resonance peak that makes noise worse.
In ultra-low-power designs, capacitor leakage or tantalum short-circuit failure can matter, and in audio or sensitive analog, high-K ceramics can be microphonic.

Third, when it's the wrong tool: you don't put a capacitor on a data or analog signal to 'decouple' it, because that's a low-pass filter on the signal, and you shouldn't add capacitance on a high-impedance feedback or sense node without checking the loop.
So I'd check the datasheet, model the hot-plug or loop if there's any doubt, and use filtering deliberately where I want it."
